beats.narration: Begin by framing Foundations of Parallel Architectures as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Consider this worked case: A multi-core processor shares a single memory space, while a distributed cluster connects independent machines over a network to solve large-scale problems. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Foundations of Parallel Architectures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a side-by-side diagram comparing a single multi-core CPU with a networked cluster of independent nodes, highlighting memory locality versus network communication.

beats.narration: Now define Distributed-Memory Process Organization precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Distributed-memory programs must partition data and work, communicate required dependencies, and avoid deadlock. Consider this worked case: In a MPI program, each process holds a unique segment of an array and must explicitly send and receive data to complete a global computation. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Distributed-Memory Process Organization
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart of data partitioning across four processes, with arrows indicating message passing and a highlighted deadlock scenario with circular waits.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how MPI Communication Mechanisms operates in a concrete sequence. MPI defines communication among processes identified by ranks in communicators. Consider this worked case: A broadcast sends a single message from one rank to all others, while a reduction combines values from all ranks into a single result. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: MPI Communication Mechanisms
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a star topology for a broadcast and a tree topology for a reduction, labeling each node with its rank and the direction of data flow.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Blocking and Nonblocking Operations and make the decision criteria explicit. Blocking and nonblocking operations expose different completion and overlap behavior. Consider this worked case: A nonblocking send allows a process to continue executing independent tasks while the message is transmitted, improving pipeline efficiency. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Blocking and Nonblocking Operations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a timeline showing a blocking operation halting execution until completion versus a nonblocking operation allowing overlapping computation and communication.

beats.narration: Apply Shared-Memory Parallel Programming to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. OpenMP defines a shared-memory parallel programming model based on directives, library routines, and environment variables. Consider this worked case: A parallel region directive spawns multiple threads that execute concurrently within the same address space, sharing variables unless explicitly marked otherwise. private variable scopes. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Shared-Memory Parallel Programming
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a single CPU core with multiple thread execution contexts branching from a parallel region, showing shared vs. private variable scopes.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Worksharing and Data Sharing, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Data-sharing attributes determine whether variables are shared, private, firstprivate, or reduced across threads. Consider this worked case: A firstprivate clause copies a variable to each thread, ensuring independent execution without race conditions, whereas a shared clause allows concurrent access. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Worksharing and Data Sharing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a table mapping data-sharing attributes to thread behavior, with icons indicating private copies versus shared memory access.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Synchronization and Data Races with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Barriers and other synchronization constructs establish ordering where independent execution is not sufficient. Consider this worked case: A barrier forces all threads to wait until every thread reaches the same point, preventing one thread from reading uninitialized data. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Synchronization and Data Races
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a race condition scenario where two threads write to the same variable without a barrier, resulting in corrupted output, then show the corrected version with a barrier.

beats.narration: Use Performance Analysis Metrics to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Performance analysis considers communication volume, latency, load balance, synchronization, process placement, and the ratio of useful work to coordination overhead. Consider this worked case: A poorly load-balanced cluster wastes resources when some nodes finish early and idle while others process remaining work. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Performance Analysis Metrics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a bar chart comparing communication overhead versus useful computation across different process placements, highlighting the optimal ratio.

beats.narration: Connect Scalability and Concurrency Evaluation to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Parallel analysis distinguishes available concurrency, task granularity, dependencies, synchronization cost, memory behavior, and measured scalability. Consider this worked case: Fine-grained tasks increase concurrency but raise synchronization costs, while coarse-grained tasks reduce overhead but limit available concurrency. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Scalability and Concurrency Evaluation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Plot a graph showing scalability efficiency against task granularity, marking the optimal region where synchronization cost is minimized.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Incorrectly synchronized accesses can create data races. Consider this worked case: A checklist confirms that MPI ranks are correctly mapped, OpenMP barriers are placed after shared variable updates, and load distribution is balanced across all nodes. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a printable checklist template with checkboxes for deadlock avoidance, model alignment, and race condition prevention, ready for student use.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: This course is an introduction to the organization and programming of systems comprising multiple computers. Topics include the organization of multi-core computers, parallel computer clusters, computing grids, client-server systems, and peer-to-peer systems; computer networks and network protocols; network security; multi-threaded programming; and network programming. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

sources.author: OpenMP Architecture Review Board
sources.excerpt: OpenMP defines a shared-memory parallel programming model based on directives, library routines, and environment variables. A parallel region creates a team of threads. Worksharing constructs divide loop iterations or sections among the team. Data-sharing attributes determine whether variables are shared, private, firstprivate, or reduced across threads. Barriers and other synchronization constructs establish ordering where independent execution is not sufficient. Incorrectly synchronized accesses can create data races. Scheduling choices influence load balance, locality, and overhead. Parallel analysis distinguishes available concurrency, task granularity, dependencies, synchronization cost, memory behavior, and measured scalability.

sources.author: Message Passing Interface Forum
sources.excerpt: MPI defines communication among processes identified by ranks in communicators. Point-to-point operations send and receive typed messages between selected ranks. Collective operations coordinate communication patterns such as broadcast, reduction, gather, scatter, and barrier across a group. Blocking and nonblocking operations expose different completion and overlap behavior. Message matching depends on communicator, source, and tag. Distributed-memory programs must partition data and work, communicate required dependencies, and avoid deadlock. Performance analysis considers communication volume, latency, load balance, synchronization, process placement, and the ratio of useful work to coordination overhead.
